description: Israel/Church addressed as singular or plural collectively
hint: When addressing Israel or the Church collectively, the grammatical number may shift between singular (unified body) and plural (individual members). Deuteronomy 6 uses singular 'you' addressing Israel as one people. Target language should maintain this collective singular if possible - it emphasizes covenant unity with God.

description: Direct speech from God - often uses exclusive first person
hint: Divine speech uses first person ('I AM', 'I created'). When God says 'us/our' (Gen 1:26, 3:22), prefer Trial if language has it (Trinity = 3 persons). The shift from singular 'I' to plural 'us' in divine speech often indicates Trinitarian self-reference. Never use Dual for Trinity contexts - Dual implies only 2 persons (Arianism).

Commands may be singular (to individual) or plural (to group). Hebrew/Greek imperative number matches the addressee. The two tablets of stone (Dual) vs the commandments themselves (Plural/Singular depending on grouping). Check context for whether command addresses one person or many.

Incarnation passages describe Christ as one person with two natures (divine and human). Number should typically be Singular - Christ is ONE person. 'The Word' (John 1) is Singular even though the Word was God. Watch for collective contexts ('every knee' - Plural) vs. Christ himself (Singular).

description: Messianic prophecies - may have complex person/number patterns
hint: Messianic prophecies often use Singular for the promised Messiah ('a child', 'a virgin', 'he was pierced'). The Messiah is consistently portrayed as one individual. Isaiah 53's 'he' pronouns are Singular referring to Christ. Don't be confused by collective interpretations - Christian orthodoxy maintains Singular messianic references.

description: Poetic/wisdom literature - may have unusual structures
hint: Hebrew poetry uses parallelism which may alternate singular/plural for stylistic effect. 'The heavens declare' - Hebrew shamayim has dual morphology but often Singular meaning (one sky). Body part pairs (eyes, hands, feet) use Dual. Generic statements ('the man who...') typically Singular. Angels/nations praising typically Plural.

description: Prayer contexts - addressee is typically God
hint: Prayer typically addresses God in second person Singular ('You' = one God). Collective prayers may use first person Plural ('we', 'our'). When the Psalms call on angels/nations to praise, those subjects are Plural. The object of worship (God/Yahweh) remains Singular. Watch for shifts between individual ('my soul') and communal ('let us praise').

description: Verses involving Trinitarian theology - plural forms referring to the one God
hint: Trinity passages: When Father/Son/Spirit are referenced together or God uses 'us/our', prefer Trial (3 persons) if available, otherwise Plural. NEVER use Dual - implies only 2 persons (heretical). Matthew 28:19 'name' (Singular!) of Father/Son/Spirit emphasizes ONE God in three persons. 'Yahweh is one' (Deut 6:4) - Singular affirms monotheism even with Trinitarian references.

description: Verses not matched to any theological grouping - needs manual review
hint: These verses don't have special theological significance for number. Use standard grammatical analysis: count the entities, use Singular for 1, Dual for 2, Trial for 3, Paucal for few (3-10), Plural for many. Check Hebrew/Greek morphology when available. Default to most natural number in target language unless context specifies exact count.
